opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and honestly something I think about a lot, maybe more than I think about any specific paper.

When you're running a research group, or now a small startup team, people look to you not only for ideas but for a kind of emotional temperature. If I come into a meeting tired or uncertain, everybody feels it immediately. If I come in excited about some weird result, even a failed experiment, that excitement spreads too. So I've come to see part of my job as being a kind of battery, or maybe a source of conviction.

Research is mostly failure. Ninety percent of what my students try doesn't work. If the person leading the group treats every failure as a disaster, people get scared and conservative, and they stop taking the risks that actually lead somewhere interesting. So I try to keep the energy about curiosity, not outcomes. "Okay, this didn't work. Why? What does it tell us about the world?" That framing matters a lot, especially for younger students who haven't built up their own resilience yet.

But I've also learned that you can't fake it. If I pretend to be excited about something I don't believe in, students see through it very quickly. They're smart. So the energy has to come from real conviction. That's one reason I try to work on problems I truly care about, like visual understanding, world models, and how intelligence is grounded in the physical world, rather than whatever is trendy that month. If I believe in the direction, the energy is natural.

With the startup it's a bit different. In academia, energy is about protecting long-term exploration. In a company there's more pressure: timelines, resources, competition. Being a source of energy there also means being a buffer. I try to absorb some of the anxiety from outside so the team can focus. People do their best work when they feel safe enough to think deeply, not when they're panicking about the next deadline.

And it goes both ways. I get a lot of energy from my students. When someone shows me a result I didn't expect, or argues with me and turns out to be right, that's what makes this whole thing fun. So it's less me giving energy and more me keeping the cycle going, so it doesn't die out when things get hard.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes motivating his students and team, and says he gets energy from his students, but never mentions Yann or passing on energy he received from Yann.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of myself as a battery that everyone plugs into. If I did, I'd burn out in a month, and so would they. What I try to do is something closer to being a thermostat than a furnace.

With students, the energy has to come from the problem, not from me. My job is to help them find a question that genuinely bothers them, something they can't stop thinking about in the shower. Once that happens, I almost get out of the way. I've seen advisors who push students very hard and the student produces a lot of papers, and then the moment they graduate, they stop. That's not energy, that's borrowed energy, and it has to be paid back. What I want is for the student to leave with their own engine running.

That said, there is a real thing I owe them, which is conviction. Research is mostly failure. Ninety percent of the experiments don't work, reviewers are harsh, and there's always a bigger lab with more GPUs. In those moments, a student doesn't need me to be excited, they need me to be calm and to say: this direction is still right, let's look at why it didn't work. Steadiness is a form of energy too, maybe the most important one.

The startup team is a different rhythm. In a lab, you can afford to be patient and wander, and that wandering is actually the point. In a company, the clock is loud. The energy I'm supposed to supply there is more about clarity, saying clearly what we're betting on and what we're not doing, so people aren't spending their energy on anxiety. A team that knows the bet is right can work very hard without feeling drained. A team that doesn't know what the bet is gets exhausted even when it isn't doing much.

And I'll admit the honest part: a lot of the energy flows back to me. When a student shows me a result I didn't expect, or someone on the team argues me out of a bad idea, that's what keeps me going. So I'd say I'm less a source than a node. The energy circulates, and my role is to keep it from leaking out.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes how energy circulates among students and the startup team, but does not mention Yann or express a hope to pass on energy received from him.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of my role is to help people feel that the work is worth doing, especially when things aren’t working. In research, you can spend months on an idea and still not know whether you’re making progress. A startup has that uncertainty too, but with a different kind of pressure. People look to you for a sense of direction.

That doesn’t mean I need to be the most energetic person in every meeting or pretend I have all the answers. Sometimes the most useful thing I can say is, “I don’t know either, but here’s how we can figure it out.” You take a big, ambiguous problem and help the team find a concrete next step.

With students, I also want to leave room for them to develop their own judgment. If all the motivation comes from me, that’s not sustainable. Ideally, they find a question they care about enough that they start pulling me into it. And that happens—their excitement gives me energy too. So I see it as something we build together, rather than something I’m constantly supplying.

r001.rationale: The response describes building motivation together with students and helping the team find direction, but it does not mention Yann or express a hope to pass on energy he received from Yann.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of my role is to create an environment where people feel excited to try things. Research has a lot of uncertainty. You can work on something for months and it doesn’t work, and at that point, people don’t necessarily need you to give them another idea. Sometimes they need you to help them see why the question is still interesting, and why it’s worth taking the next step.

But being a source of energy doesn’t mean being positive all the time. If something isn’t working, we should talk about it honestly. I want people to feel that we can face a difficult result together, learn something, and keep moving.

And that energy goes both ways. When a student shows me something unexpected, or someone on the team challenges an assumption, I get excited too. Ideally, you build a team where curiosity and ownership are shared, so the energy doesn’t depend on one person.

r001.rationale: The response describes creating and sharing energy with students and teammates, but does not say that Xie received motivating energy from Yann or hopes to pass that energy on.
